opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is that the mission itself is something they've been waiting for. If you talk to a lot of serious mathematicians, many of them have been thinking for years about what it would mean for machines to genuinely reason, not just pattern-match, but produce proofs you can actually verify. When someone comes along and says, "We're going to build that, and we're going to take it seriously on both the math side and the AI side," that resonates. So I don't think they're joining *me* so much as joining a problem they already cared about deeply.

The second thing is that I try to speak their language. I came up through mathematics, and I still think of myself as a mathematician at heart. When I sit down with a researcher, I'm not pitching them a product deck. We talk about formal verification, about why Lean matters, about what a good benchmark actually looks like versus one that just looks impressive. I think people can tell pretty quickly whether you respect the depth of what they do, or whether you're treating math as a marketing hook.

And honestly, being young and not having a long track record can be an advantage in a strange way. I don't come in pretending to know everything. My job as CEO is to clear the path: get the compute, get the resources, build an environment where really strong people can do the most ambitious work of their careers without the bureaucracy they might face elsewhere. Senior researchers have often spent years in settings where they had to fight for that kind of freedom. If I can offer it, and pair it with a clear, very concrete goal, that's quite attractive.

Finally, I'd say timing matters. We're at a moment where the tools, the models, the formal proof languages, they're all finally mature enough that this problem feels tractable. Great people want to be in the room when something like that becomes possible. I just try to make sure our room is the one where it actually happens.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the problem feels tractable because tools and models have matured, but does not express confidence that good engineering can overcome its technical difficulties.

r003.rationale: The candidate says the mission resonates with serious mathematicians who have long cared about machine reasoning and verifiable proofs, and describes the problem as attracting great researchers.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's less about me as a CEO and more about the problem we're working on. If you go to a serious mathematician and say, "I want to build a system that can actually do mathematics, not just pattern-match on it," that's a question they've been thinking about their whole lives. Formal verification, automated reasoning, whether a machine can find a proof a human hasn't found — these aren't new questions to them. What's new is that it's suddenly plausible to make real progress, and they can feel that.

The second thing is that I didn't come to them as an outsider. I did mathematics, I understand what it feels like to spend months on a lemma, I know what they care about and what they're skeptical of. When someone from a pure AI background walks into a math department and says "we're going to automate you," the reaction is usually polite but cold. If instead you say, "here's a concrete thing we can do together, and you'll be able to check every step because it's all in Lean," the conversation is completely different. They can verify what we produce. That matters enormously to mathematicians — they don't want to take anything on faith.

And then I think there's a generational piece. A lot of the senior people I talk to are genuinely curious. They've watched the field shift and they'd rather be inside the room shaping how these tools get built than reading about it afterward. Many of them have students who are already using these systems. They want to make sure the mathematics stays rigorous while that's happening.

Finally, I'd say I try to be very clear about what I don't know. I'm young, I haven't run a large organization before, and I say that openly. What I can offer is a sharp focus on the problem, the ability to move quickly, and real respect for their expertise. Experienced people, in my experience, respond well to that. They don't need you to pretend to be more than you are. They need you to be serious about the work.

r003.rationale: The response says experienced mathematicians are drawn by the problem itself: building a system that can do mathematics and make progress on questions they have long considered.

But my sense is that people are willing to work with someone when they find the problem compelling and believe that person can help them make progress. As CEO, I don’t need to be the strongest mathematician in the room. I need to listen carefully, be honest about what I don’t know, and create an environment where their expertise can shape what we do. That trust has to be earned through working together.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you’d have to ask them individually, but my sense is that it’s about the problems we’re trying to solve and the environment we can create. When someone has spent years doing research, they know how rare it is to have the time, resources, and collaborators to pursue an ambitious idea seriously.

My job as CEO is to make that possible: bring together people who challenge each other, listen carefully to their judgment, and remove obstacles so they can do their best work. I don’t think I need to know more than everyone in the room. I need to earn their trust by making good decisions and following through.
